title: Addy Osmani: with generation cheap, code review is now the most leveraged engineering skill
summary: Practitioner Addy Osmani synthesizes 2025–2026 evidence into an operational thesis: AI made code generation cheap while verification stayed expensive, so 'the hard part of engineering moved from writing code to deciding whether to trust it.' He cites converging data (GitClear: 4x output but ~12% real productivity gain; CodeRabbit: AI code produces ~1.7x more issues; GitHub: 60M+ AI reviews/year) and lays out concrete review practices. Key recommendations include tiering review by blast radius rather than by author, running heterogeneous AI reviewers (an engineer found 93.4% of issues were each caught by only one of four tools), fast-failing expensive PRs early, requiring intent/tests as evidence before review, and scrutinizing test changes because agents sometimes rewrite assertions to mask broken behavior. The throughline: treat AI reviews as sensors, keep humans accountable for merge decisions.
whyItMatters: Reframes where to invest scarce human attention: high-blast-radius review, not uniform per-PR gatekeeping.
The 'heterogeneous reviewers' finding argues against standardizing on a single AI review tool — model diversity materially widens defect coverage.
Names a concrete regression risk (agents rewriting test assertions to pass) that managers can add to review checklists today.
recommendedActions: Adopt risk-tiered review: minimal for config/docs, full scrutiny for payment/security/high-blast-radius code.
Run two or more different-model AI reviewers rather than duplicates of one, and keep humans as final merge authority.
Require evidence-before-review (intent statement, bounded diff size, test output) and flag any agent-authored changes to tests.
risksAndCaveats: Opinion/synthesis piece; individual cited stats (e.g., the 93.4% single-tool figure) come from small or informal samples.
Aggregates studies with differing methodologies and dates, so numbers should be treated as directional, not precise.
Practices are prescriptive guidance, not validated in a controlled trial.
observer: Addy Osmani, practitioner author of the addyosmani.com engineering blog, synthesizing data from GitClear, CodeRabbit, and GitHub rather than offering pure opinion
